summary: Give the FHA loan calculator the home price, the down payment percentage, the loan term and the interest rate and it returns total cost of loan. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the FHA loan calculator work?
sections.html:
The FHA loan calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total cost of loan in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the home price, the down payment percentage, the loan term and the interest rate.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the FHA loan calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

FHA base loan amount=(home price − (down payment percentage × home price))
Your down payment=(down payment percentage × home price)
Periodic interest rate=((1 ÷ 12) × interest rate)
Monthly mortgage payment=((((1 ÷ 12) × interest rate) + 1, (12 × loan term)) × ((1 ÷ 12) × interest rate) × (home price − (down payment percentage × home price)) ÷ ((((1 ÷ 12) × interest rate) + 1, (12 × loan term)) − 1))
Number of payments=(12 × loan term)
FHA Upfront MIP=((7 ÷ 400) × (home price − (down payment percentage × home price)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • %, opening in percent
  • Time, opening in years
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The FHA loan calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the home price, the down payment percentage and the loan term — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

faq.q: What does the FHA loan calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total cost of loan, derived from the home price, the down payment percentage and the loan term. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the FHA loan calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the home price, the down payment percentage, the loan term and the interest rate, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter home price in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Home price opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Your down payment = 20000. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the FHA loan calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
